nodes.description: Because UBE2A supplies the E2 activity that cooperates with the E3 ligase Parkin to ubiquitinate proteins on damaged mitochondria, loss of UBE2A impairs Parkin-dependent mitophagy, the selective autophagic clearance of dysfunctional mitochondria. The authors identify UBE2A/RAD6A as a regulator of this pathway.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations in the intellectual disability gene Ube2a cause neuronal dysfunction and impair parkin-dependent mitophagy.
evidence.snippet: Hence, we identify RAD6A as a regulator of Parkin-dependent mitophagy and establish a critical role for RAD6A in maintaining neuronal function.

nodes.description: UBE2A/RAD6A is an E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme that charges and transfers ubiquitin to substrates in concert with E3 ligases. Loss-of-function variants reduce this conjugating activity, so substrate ubiquitination that depends on UBE2A fails. A central UBE2A-dependent pathway is Parkin-mediated ubiquitination of mitochondrial proteins, the step that marks damaged mitochondria for removal.

nodes.description: The cellular consequence of mitochondrial failure in neurons is impaired synaptic function, shown directly in the dRad6-deficient Drosophila model where the synaptic defect is a consequence of the mitochondrial failure (the evidence for this sits on the incoming edge from the mitochondrial node).

The organism-level behavioural readout of UBE2A loss in the knockout mouse is a major spatial learning deficit; the authors frame this as a causal role of UBE2A in learning and mGluR-dependent long-term depression. Notably, epilepsy and motor coordination were normal in this knockout, so the mouse does not model the human seizure phenotype (recorded as a human/model mismatch in the discussions block).

nodes.description: A hemizygous loss-of-function lesion in UBE2A (Xq24) is the initiating event. Reported alleles span nonsense and frameshift mutations, missense variants at evolutionarily conserved residues, splice variants, and whole-gene or larger Xq24 deletions. The founding family carried the nonsense allele Q128X (c.382C>T), which removes the 25 C-terminal residues; their importance for UBE2 function is inferred from their conservation across vertebrates and Drosophila. Recognisable missense alleles such as G23R affect the conserved N-terminus. Both truncating and missense alleles converge on reduced or abolished ubiquitin-conjugating activity, i.e. a loss-of-function mechanism.

evidence.snippet: We report a mutation of UBE2A/HR6A, which encodes a ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme (E2), a member of the ubiquitin proteasome pathway, as the cause of a novel X-linked mental retardation (XLMR) syndrome that affects three males in a two-generation family.

evidence.snippet: Thus, both missense and truncating mutations can give rise to a specific, syndromic form of XLMR which is identifiable in a clinical setting.
